title: Asahi Kasei opens new facility for wet-process battery separators - electrive.com
content:
Japanese chemical company Asahi Kasei has opened a new coating line for Hipore wet-process battery separators in Charlotte, North Carolina, USA. The facility marks the first step in establishing a regional supply structure for wet-process plants.
Hipore separators by Asahi Kasei
Image: Asahi Kasei
The new facility has been constructed on the existing Celgard plant premises and is scheduled to begin commercial production in the second half of fiscal 2026. This investment coincides with the 40th anniversary of the Celgard site, where dry-process separators have primarily been manufactured to date.
Through this new facility and a concurrently developed
separator factory in Canada
, Asahi Kasei aims to significantly expand its local supply chain in North America. This expansion will enable the company to respond flexibly and directly to rising demand for components used in battery-electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems (ESS) in the region.
“Opening the Charlotte coating line is a key milestone in establishing our North American supply platform for battery separators,” said Ryu Taniguchi, President of Asahi Kasei Battery Separator Corporation. “By leveraging Celgard’s experienced workforce and established operations, we are expanding our North American product portfolio to include both Celgard dry-process and Hipore wet-process technologies. Together with our planned separator facility in Canada, this investment will bring production capabilities closer to the region’s battery market and position Asahi Kasei to swiftly respond as demand grows across electric vehicles and energy storage systems.”
A battery separator is an extremely thin, microporous plastic membrane placed inside a lithium-ion battery cell as an essential insulating layer between the positive electrode (cathode) and the negative electrode (anode). Its primary function is to prevent physical short circuits – thus avoiding uncontrolled heating or destruction of the cell – while simultaneously allowing lithium ions to flow through its tiny pores. This ion flow, facilitated by the liquid electrolyte, is critical for power generation.

title: SK Innovation reacquires separator subsidiary SKIET - electrive.com
content:
SK Innovation and its subsidiary SK IE Technology (SKIET), which handles the separator business, will merge. Through the merger, set to take effect on 1 January 2027, SK Innovation plans to reorganise SKIET’s separator business within the parent company.
SKIET is a highly specialised company that produces lithium-ion battery separators (LiBS), a critical component of battery cells. Originally a wholly owned subsidiary of South Korean conglomerate SK Innovation, the company was spun off in 2019 and listed on the stock exchange in 2021. However, SKIET has faced significant challenges amid slower electric vehicle market growth, delayed demand recovery in key markets such as North America and intense price competition from Chinese manufacturers.
SK Innovation says bringing SKIET back under its corporate umbrella and ending its independent listed status will strengthen financial stability, mitigate business and financial risks and improve operational efficiency. The merger is also intended to strengthen the separator business over the medium to long term and increase shareholder value. SKIET currently supplies separators to SK Innovation subsidiary SK On as well as
external customers such as LG
The merger is expected to be approved on 24 November by the SK Innovation board of directors and the SKIET general meeting, with the relevant procedural steps to be completed by the merger’s effective date of 1 January 2027. The new shares of SK Innovation issued as part of the merger will be listed on the stock exchange on 18 January 2027.
Following the merger, the company expects to improve operational efficiency within the separator business and reduce costs associated with duplicated structures. Additionally, by combining SK Innovation’s R&D capabilities with SKIET’s product development expertise, the competitiveness of the separator business is expected to strengthen – particularly through the planned expansion into separators for energy storage systems (ESS).
A representative of SK Innovation stated: “Through this merger, we plan to strengthen our financial stability and streamline our business structure, thereby enhancing the mid- to long-term competitiveness of the separator business.” The representative added: “We will do our utmost to ensure that this merger leads to a recovery in business competitiveness and an enhancement of shareholder value.”

title: Organic Flow Batteries in Steel Tanks | Battery Technology
content:
Design & Manufacturing
Stationary Batteries
Battery News
Interviews
California startup Quino Energy is repurposing underutilized oil storage tanks along the Gulf Coast to deploy quinone-based flow batteries that offer non-flammable, long-duration energy storage at gigawatt-hour scale.
August 26, 2026
8 Min Read
Oil storage tanks near the Valero Houston refinery in Houston, Texas.
Brandon Bell/Getty Images
At a Glance
Quino's quinone electrolyte is the only organic flow battery chemistry that doesn't corrode carbon steel storage tanks.
Large steel tanks enable organic flow batteries to reach energy densities 2-3 times higher than lithium-ion systems.
Technology uses abundant materials like quinone and ferrocyanide, avoiding critical mineral supply chain concerns.
As demand for long-duration energy storage grows across the United States, one California startup is pioneering an innovative approach to battery energy storage systems (BESS). Quino Energy's organic flow batteries use quinone-based electrolytes that can be stored in repurposed steel oil tanks, offering a non-flammable alternative to lithium-ion batteries for grid-scale applications. This breakthrough could transform underutilized energy infrastructure along the Gulf Coast into vital components of the nation's energy transition.
Clustered predominately throughout subterranean salt caverns along the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana, an allotment of reserve tanks for emergency crude oil sits empty and unused. Although unpredictable circumstances such as international conflict and increasingly dangerous weather patterns influence the availability of these vacant, valuable resources, it stands to reason that the growing presence of electric vehicles will consistently free up tanks for other potential purposes — perhaps the storage of power and electricity?
Related:
How CATL Moved Sodium-Ion Batteries From Lab Chemistry to GWh-Scale Reality
Repurposing steel oil tanks for battery energy storage systems
"Tank storage infrastructure is being adversely affected by the energy transition," said Eugene Beh, chief executive officer and cofounder of
Quino Energy
, a clean-tech startup company based in San Leandro, CA. "Meanwhile, demand for resilient, reliable short-to-long-duration energy infrastructure grows each day as more data centers come online and as the global energy transition impacts the grid."
As a variable assortment of these steel tanks remain underutilized, Beh sees a possibility to scale up domestic battery production and strengthen supply chains while boosting energy dominance in the United States with a resource that is seemingly up for grabs for suitable products, such as the battery energy storage system (BESS) produced at Quino that utilizes an organic molecule known as a quinone to store power.
Quino Energy's quinone-based flow battery technology
Capable of easily switching between oxidized and reduced states, the quinone is ideal for use in redox flow batteries, said Beh. He also sees his company's BESS being well-suited for many developing needs, including data center applications and other projects, when compared to lithium-ion and other common alternatives, given the high water solubility, chemical stability, and cycling capabilities that these flow batteries provide.
Quino Energy's zero-waste organic electrolyte production system in Buffalo, NY. Credit: Quino Energy
Following the close of $10 million in a Series A funding round from Atri Energy Transition this past fall and a grant awarded through the CarbonX program by global technology company Tencent, Beh said Quino Energy is positioned to take advantage of its growing resources and unique technologies to be competitive in the "energy density race" as a dark horse while more people become knowledgeable about the potential of organic flow batteries.
Related:
How Battery Validation is Shaping the Future Grid
How organic flow batteries work: An empowering electrolyte
Although the popularity and market adoption of flow batteries continues to increase as utility companies, industrial microgrid operators, solar and wind farms, and other stakeholders invest more in long-duration energy storage, flow batteries remain relatively unknown in the Western world when compared to "conventional" lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries, says Beh.
"While approximately four gigawatt hours of new flow battery capacity was installed in 2025, the vast majority of deployments took place in China," he said. "And there is now growing awareness that flow batteries can be a good option for data center builds or other locations originally thought to be unsuitable for battery energy storage systems because of the advantages offered in terms of cycle life and non-flammability."
Why steel tank compatibility matters for energy storage
But not all electrolytes are equal, and the unique nature of the organic properties found in the Quino BESS offers benefits that go beyond the typical amenities of flow batteries that contain such elements as vanadium, iron, zinc/bromine, and iron/chromium that would not be chemically compatible with the carbon steel most commonly used to construct the available tanks.
Related:
Startups Pitch Investors to Transform the Battery Industry
"The electrolytes must not be acidic in nature," Beh explained. "Furthermore, they must not contain any chlorides, which are highly corrosive to steel, and therefore ruling out every other organic flow battery technology that we are aware of because they rely on chloride as a mobile ion during battery cycling. We believe that Quino Energy's electrolyte is the only commercially mature electrolyte that is compatible with steel tanks."
The electrical connections to Quino Energy's electrochemical reactor help to enable the BESS zero-waste organic electrolyte production system. Credit: Quino Energy
During the International Flow Battery Forum in Budapest, Hungary, this past June, Beh and colleagues presented data that displayed very low or "undetectable" corrosion rates of two common grades of carbon steel commonly used in storage tanks with the Quino electrolytes. Data also reportedly showed the measured corrosion rates allowed a service life of more than 10 years without any kind of protective coating or surface treatment.
Cost-effective grid-scale energy storage solutions
"We believe our battery electrolyte could be stored in the tanks without needing any surface treatment or protection on the steel, avoiding the need to update or build a new infrastructure and reducing the expenditure of time, labor, and financial resources associated with new installations," said Beh. "There are also plenty of underutilized tanks that are fully depreciated that could be easily repurposed into large flow batteries."
As of mid-August, Beh said he and his colleagues were in the process of evaluating immediate opportunities to implement steel tanks into flow batteries, which he says would create an industry-first method and support a more cost-effective deployment of long-duration energy storage at the gigawatt-hour scale.
Repurposing tank infrastructure would represent an innovation in installation costs and time to completion, complementing parallel reductions in organic flow battery capital expenditure, says Beh. Additionally, the largest class of tanks would enable organic flow batteries to reach energy densities that measure 2-3 times more than equivalent lithium-ion, he said.
"Flow batteries are commonly thought to have low energy density, but that is only true when it comes to weight," said Beh. "Individual lithium-ion battery packs must be spaced apart to prevent fire propagation and cannot be stacked vertically, but flow battery electrolytes have no such limitation. The large tank form factor would allow organic flow batteries to reach much higher energy densities."
The non-flammable elements would also conceivably protect infrastructure, facilities and employees, and communities that sit downwind from potential fires. "And these systems can be manufactured using readily available materials free of supply chain and trade concerns, enabling faster project timelines," said Beh. "Organic flow battery electrolytes don't rely on critical minerals and materials. They can leverage mature, existing vanadium flow battery hardware – minus the vanadium – that is already being produced at the gigawatt scale."
Understanding flow battery technology: A promising alternative
Generally speaking, Beh likens the flow battery to a gasoline automobile: An intake of air is delivered to the engine to be mixed with fuel to create a combustion that powers the vehicle. The air oxidizes the fuel and is combined within the engine to cause the reaction of energy.
With a flow battery, two tanks of liquid — a fuel, so to speak, and an oxidizer — are dissolved in a solvent, which is water for many of the batteries. Both are pumped simultaneously to a power block that resembles a fuel cell but doesn't use platinum or other catalysts.
"The fuel and oxidizer liquids are pumped to the power block, and they can get reacted there, which gives you electricity out," Beh explains. "The spent fuel and spent oxidizer are retained in the tanks, and when you put electricity into the power block you can get the reverse chemical reaction to happen. That's how you can take electricity back into chemical energy. And that's basically the reverse reaction that's charging the battery."
Quinone and ferrocyanide: Abundant materials for energy storage
Distinguishing the organic flow battery from lithium-ion batteries and the vanadium electrolyte that typically exists among other flow batteries is that the development of Quino's BESS does not require any fluorinated or critical materials to manufacture, as all elements are considered to be abundant raw materials, according to Beh.
The quinone serves as the negative electrolyte, or the fuel, with ferrocyanide, a common additive to table salt and de-icing salt, serving the role of the positive electrolyte, or the oxidizer. Both are dissolved in an aqueous solution and can replace vanadium and other expensive critical minerals commonly used in traditional flow batteries, said Beh.
Credit: Quino Energy
"Thus, complications associated with critical material supply chains, such as impacts from geopolitical tensions, trade, and tariff complications, which often impact imports of materials like lithium and vanadium, do not impact organic flow battery development and deployment anywhere close to the same extent," said Beh.
Safety and environmental benefits of non-flammable flow batteries
Flow batteries have the additional distinction of receiving unique permit thresholds, spill control mandates, and maximum allowable quantities that impact fire and building code requirements, including the International Fire Code and NFPA's standards for installation of stationary energy storage systems. These regulations remain separate from those of lithium-ion and lead-acid cells, and are expected to evolve for the better over time, said Beh.
"Being completely non-flammable, flow batteries are not subject to fire risks or plumes of toxic smoke, as is the case with lithium-ion battery fires," he said. As such, many of the siting, monitoring, and response considerations would not be required or would become irrelevant. A different set of guidelines could be needed.
"The shortcomings of lithium-ion batteries are well-known," said Beh. "These have created an opportunity for a compact, non-flammable battery technology like organic flow batteries to prove themselves."

title: Sedex Launches Regulatory Navigator for Supply Chains
content:
Sedex Launches Regulatory Navigator for Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Sedex's new tool gives teams a steer on which supply chain due diligence and sustainability regulations apply to them (Image source: Sedex)
As CSDDD and CSRD thresholds shift and forced labour rules tighten, Sedex has launched a tool to help teams track what applies
Supply chain regulation has not stood still so far this year. The EU finalised sweeping changes to two flagship sustainability laws, forced labour import bans spread across three continents and several countries have come under diplomatic pressure to tighten their own rules, all within a few months.
Against that backdrop, Sedex, a global supply chain sustainability solutions provider, has launched the Regulatory Navigator, a free self-serve tool giving businesses an indicative view of which major supply chain due diligence and sustainability regulations apply to them.
The tool launched on 25 August, arriving as compliance, procurement and sustainability teams face a growing
volume of overlapping legislation
, from the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) to forced labour product bans.
A regulatory landscape in flux
The scope of Europe's two flagship sustainability laws changed significantly this year. In February 2026, the amended CSDDD was published, raising its threshold from 1,000 to more than 5,000 employees and from €450m to more than €1.5bn in global net turnover, cutting the number of in-scope companies by around 70%.
Mandatory climate transition plans
were dropped and compliance was pushed back to July 2029.
The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) also had a similar rebalancing, seeing it now apply only to companies with more than 1,000 employees and €450m or more in net turnover, in turn cutting the number of in-scope companies by almost 85%.
Businesses don't need complexity: they need clarity. The Regulatory Navigator helps teams move from uncertainty to informed action faster and
develop a centralised compliance roadmap
that avoids duplicating the common tasks required, such as mapping supply chain risks across multiple tiers.
Jon Hancock, Chief Executive Officer at Sedex
Forced labour enforcement has moved in the opposite direction, tightening rather than narrowing. The European Commission must establish a forced labour risk database by 14 June 2026 ahead of its Forced Labour Regulation taking effect in December 2027.
Canada introduced draft legislation in June 2026 to strengthen its import ban with new supply chain tracing requirements. In the US, the Trade Representative imposed tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on 60 trading partners in July 2026 over their failure to enforce forced labour import bans, prompting Indonesia, Pakistan and El Salvador to introduce their own.
For teams tracking obligations across multiple markets, that combination of
narrowing EU thresholds
and tightening forced labour rules elsewhere makes it harder, not easier, to know which requirements genuinely apply.
Sedex's tool: How it works
Users are required to answer a short set of questions covering their business's headquarters, approximate annual revenue, global workforce, the markets they operate in and whether they import goods into the EU or the US.
The tool then flags which of eight major regulations are likely to apply, each with a plain-language explanation, key thresholds and a summary of compliance requirements, as well as key deadlines.
Sedex's Regulatory Navigator works as an accessible starting point for understanding potential obligations before formal legal scoping begins (Image source: Sedex)
Regulations covered include:
the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)
the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD)
the EU Forced Labour Regulation
Canada's Fighting Against Forced Labour and Child Labour in Supply Chains Act (S-211)
Australia's Modern Slavery Act.
Its regulatory content reflects the EU Omnibus Simplification Package I, keeping CSDDD and CSRD thresholds current.
Jon Hancock, Chief Executive Officer at Sedex, says the tool responds to a wider need for clarity rather than added complexity. “Businesses don't need complexity: they need clarity,” he says.
“The Regulatory Navigator helps teams move from uncertainty to informed action faster and develop a centralised compliance roadmap that avoids duplicating the common tasks required, such as mapping supply chain risks across multiple tiers."
Maurizio Capuzzo, Chief Marketing Officer at Sedex, echoes this and frames the launch as a response to one of the most common challenges raised by the company's customers, where multiplying rules and shifting thresholds make it difficult for teams to know where to start.
Jon Hancock, Sedex CEO
Why this matters for supply chain leaders
The Regulatory Navigator gives compliance,
procurement
, sustainability and supply chain teams an accessible starting point for understanding potential obligations before formal legal scoping begins.
That starting point matters most for multinational organisations juggling overlapping requirements across the EU, UK, Canada, Australia and the US, where a single sourcing decision can now trigger several regulatory regimes at once, some narrowing in scope and others tightening enforcement in the same year.
It is important to note that Sedex is clear that results are indicative only, and are not a substitute for legal advice.
Key partner cited: Sedex
Sedex is a global supply chain
sustainability solutions provider
, headquartered in London with an additional base in Chicago. Jon Hancock serves as Chief Executive Officer, with Maurizio Capuzzo as Chief Marketing Officer. Sedex provides tools and data supporting responsible sourcing, ethical trade and supply chain due diligence for businesses managing multi-tier supplier networks.

title: Breedr Drives Traceability in Global Beef Supply Chain
content:
Breedr Drives Traceability in Global Beef Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
Breedr is digitising the global beef supply chain in order to drive traceability and efficiency. Credit: Unsplash
Breedr has raised US$27m in Series B funding, with an aim of digitising the global beef supply chain, encouraging traceability and driving sustainability
The beef supply chain is a significant one, though it is not always thought about. It involves moving cattle from farms to processing plants, before it reaches consumers.
A major concern within beef supply chains is the reduction of emissions – beef production generates high greenhouse gas emissions, involves significant water consumption and land use changes. This translates to
high methane emissions
, ongoing deforestation and significant resource usage.
Breedr, the platform giving each cow a digital record, is aiming to change the game with its increased traceability efforts. Alongside the announcement of its US$27m in Series B funding, the platform is aiming to transform the global
beef supply chain
Key facts
Breedr currently has two million cattle on its books
Breedr has raised US$27m in Series B funding
The aim is to create a traceable pathway for 1.3 billion cattle
Breedr estimates a 20-30% reduction in methane per animal
Funding scope
Breedr was founded in 2018, with the aim of helping farmers produce commercially and environmentally sustainable meat, thus prolonging the resilience of operations and reducing the negative environmental impact of the beef industry. Though it started small, it now has a network of thousands of farmers, working to drive forward-thinking solutions and ensure positive change.
It gives each cow a digital record, meaning it is traced from birth to the supermarket shelf. The platform operates across ten global supply chains and currently has two million cattle on its books. Almost US$500m of livestock has been transacted in the last year using the platform, and its customer base spans across family ranches and major organisations which handle more than 100,000 cattle a year. The aim of Breedr is to reach the entire beef
supply chain
, creating a traceable pathway for all 1.3 billion cattle.
Now, the platform has announced that it has raised US$27m in Series B funding. This has been led by Partech, a global technology investment organisation, through its impact fund. Partech Impact works to support organisations which are aiming to transform value chains across industry, agriculture, infrastructure, healthcare and more.
The funding round included support from Latitude, LocalGlobe and Outsiders Fund, which was a leader in the Series A funding round. Breedr now has a combined funding of US$46.6m, which will help grow the team and capabilities of the platform. With an aim of growing exponentially, the funding will help bring more ranchers and farmers to Breedr and means the company can invest in technological advancements to increase data point capturing – including genomic data.
Traceability and sustainability
are what make a beef business more productive and more profitable," Ian Wheal, Founder and CEO of Breedr, told Supply Chain Digital.
Ian Wheal, Founder and CEO of Breedr
"A supply chain that can trace an animal from birth knows exactly what its genetic history is, what it is worth and where the value is being lost. Sustainability works the same way, the most sustainable animal is usually the most efficient one, the one that puts on weight faster on less feed, and efficiency is simply another word for profit."
Increasing efficiency
Though demand for beef is constantly rising, the US cattle herd started 2026 at its lowest level since 1951, according to the United States Department of Agriculture. Moreover, this year's calf crop is expected to be the smallest on record. To make the most out of each animal and every aspect of the cattle crop, the industry needs thorough insights into the crop. Paper trails are no longer efficient for visibility, which is why Breedr increases capabilities within the sector.
The digital record uses weight, health and family history of each cow, with updates being added at each ranch the animal passes through in its lifespan.
Ian says, "We built Breedr to bring value back to the people who raise the cattle. Demand for beef is climbing while the herd is the smallest it has been in 75 years. The industry has to get more value from every animal, and you cannot do that on paper.
"If you have bought beef from a major retailer in the United States or UK, there is a good chance it has moved through a Breedr-powered supply chain. We already do the same in Australia and New Zealand, and this round enables us to expand connected supply chains globally - where every animal tells its own story and every producer gets paid for the quality they raise."
Breedr includes a dedicated marketplace where producers can trade on – instead of relying on what judges can see at an auction, they can judge using detailed data points. The app offers a thorough digital record and lower fees. It helps inform the optimum point of sale through a growth prediction model which uses AI.
The most sustainable animal is usually the most efficient one, the one that puts on weight faster on less feed, and efficiency is simply another word for profit.
Ian Wheal, Founder and CEO of Breedr
The Breedr platform offers thorough insights into each animal. Credit: Breedr
Ian explains to Supply Chain Digital: "Farmers record data now, but it's all in paper notebooks or in spreadsheets. Breedr replaces paper and best guesses with animal intelligence. A producer can see the performance of every animal, a buyer can understand exactly what they are purchasing, and nobody is doing double data entry. The result is less wasted effort and better outcomes, which means a more productive business at one end and a more profitable one at the other."
Sustainability and traceability
"Beef is one of the most complex decarbonisation problems there is. Breedr cuts emissions while helping producers become more profitable," explains Arnaud Minvielle, General Partner at Partech, who has joined Breedr's board.
Arnaud Minvielle, General Partner at Partech
"Ian and the Breedr team are building the transaction layer for one of the world’s largest unmodernised markets, earning revenue every time an animal changes hands. That alignment between the commercial engine and the environmental outcome is exactly what our impact fund exists to back. We truly believe that Ian, being an insider from this industry, and his team can fundamentally transform this value chain with data intelligence.”
Due to the streamlined transactions and monitoring, producers can earn more than US$500 per animal. This is due to the
keen insights and the traceability
of each animal, offering confidence for the buyer. Alongside this, Breeder has a cattle fund which allows producers to unlock money from animals they are still raising, meaning they can start generating income sooner.
Breedr, operating across the UK, US and Australia, offers a closed-loop system for managing livestock and cattle fund, as well as a data-verified marketplace. Through this, it drives security within the
beef supply chain
, alongside thorough insights and an increased sustainability opportunity.

title: Bafang's new electric bike motors produce 8x your own pedaling power
content:
Micah Toll
| Aug 26 2026 - 8:12 am PT
Bafang has never exactly been known for building timid e-bike motors, but its latest pair of high-performance e-MTB drives takes things to a whole new level. We’re talking up to 1,700 watts of peak power, 150 Nm of torque, and 800% pedal assistance.
At that point, “pedal assist” is starting to do some pretty heavy lifting as a phrase.
Bafang M510RS and M560RS
are production versions of motors first shown as concepts at Eurobike last year. They’re set to make their official production debut at the Italian Bike Festival in Misano, Italy, September 4-6, ahead of series production later this year.
The slightly more reasonable of the two – and I’m using “reasonable” rather generously here – is the M510RS. It offers 110 Nm of peak torque during normal operation, while Bafang’s temporary Boost-to-Limit function can push that as high as 120-130 Nm depending on the system voltage. Peak power reaches 1,100W on a 36V system or 1,300W at 48V.
Then there’s the M560RS, which is where things start getting particularly bonkers.
That motor produces 120 Nm normally, increasing to as much as 150 Nm in Boost-to-Limit mode. A 36V setup can deliver 1,400W of peak power, while the 48V version cranks that figure all the way up to 1,700W. All of that, yet the motor weighs just 3.3 kg (7.3 lb). Sure, chunky for an e-bike – but not that bad in absolute terms.
To put that into perspective, there are plenty of regular commuter e-bikes running around with 350W or 500W motors. Bafang is now stuffing several times that peak power into a compact mid-drive designed to help mountain bikers blast up nasty technical climbs.
Of course, those huge figures aren’t available continuously. Those are the peak figures. Boost-to-Limit is essentially a short-duration overdrive mode meant for particularly difficult obstacles and steep sections. But when activated, Bafang says it can provide an almost comical 800% assistance, meaning the motor can contribute eight times the rider’s own input. The less extreme Sport+ mode still offers up to 500% adaptive assistance.
And Bafang isn’t simply throwing a gigantic motor at the problem.
Both RS motors use a six-axis IMU along with torque, cadence, and wheel-speed sensing to determine what the bike and rider are doing in real time. Bafang says the RS systems react 50% faster than the standard M510 and M560 motors, while also cutting motor power 33% more sensitively. That latter figure could be especially important when you’re trying to precisely control a 150 Nm mid-drive on loose terrain. There’s also Hill Hold to keep the bike from rolling backward on steep starts and an updated Walk Assist function.
Bafang says it spent more than 4,000 hours fine-tuning the systems under racing conditions, including development through the WES UCI E-MTB World Cup series.
There’s another practical advantage hiding underneath all of those headline-grabbing power figures: the M510RS and M560RS retain the same mounting interfaces as the existing M510 and M560. That means bike manufacturers already designing around those motors won’t necessarily need to develop entirely new frames just to adopt the RS versions.
The M560RS will also be offered in versions intended for both European 25 km/h (15.5 mph) and US 45 km/h (28 mph) requirements. Of course, the peak power level blows past the limits of traditional electric bicycles for street use in most countries, but these motors are specifically for eMTBs, which means they’re designed for climbing mountains, not bike lanes.
Electrek’s Take
Inevitably, these numbers are going to draw comparisons to the e-bike motor system spun out of DJI, the
Avinox drive systems
, which have helped push high-performance e-MTB motors into increasingly absurd territory. And yes, on paper Bafang’s 1,700W figure manages to push the power envelope even farther.
But I think the more interesting story is simply how far e-bike mid-drives themselves have come. We’re now looking at relatively compact motors capable of producing 150 Nm and four-digit peak wattage while simultaneously using IMUs and multiple sensors to meter out that power pedal stroke by pedal stroke.
Whether anyone actually
1,700 watts in an electric mountain bike is another question.
But if you’ve ever looked at a ridiculously steep, loose climb and thought, “I wonder if my e-bike could get up that,” Bafang apparently wants the answer to be an emphatic yes.

title: Hyundai is about to shake things up with 100 new vehicles by 2030: Here's what's coming
content:
Hyundai Motor Group
Peter Johnson
| Aug 26 2026 - 8:06 am PT
Hyundai Motor Company
, including Genesis, is about to get very busy, with plans to launch more than 100 new or updated vehicles by 2030, including its first extended-range EVs (EREVs).
Hyundai plans new vehicle blitz with EVs and EREVS
While many are pulling back, Hyundai is going on the offensive. Hyundai announced plans to launch over 100 new or refreshed vehicles by the end of the decade during its 2026 CEO Investor Day on Wednesday.
“Our fundamentals have never been,” Hyundai’s CEO, José Muñoz, said. As the third-largest automotive group and second most profitable, Hyundai has “the ability to invest while others are pulling back,” Muñoz explained.
Hyundai will launch over 100 new vehicles globally by 2030, including 58 in North America, 49 in Korea, 41 in Europe, 26 in India, and 22 in China.
The first of which includes the new Elantra, IONIQ 3, the
new Tucson and Tucson Hybrid
, the Santa Fe EREV, a new A-segment EV SUV for India, a new global B-segment SUV, and another B-segment SUV for Europe.
Hyundai new vehicle launches by 2030 (Source: Hyundai)
The new Tucson and Tucson Hybrid will launch later this year, followed by the Santa Fe EREV in the first half of 2027, Hyundai’s first extended-range electric vehicle (EREV).
Hyundai expects the Santa Fe EREV will deliver over 600 miles of combined driving range. It uses a battery electric drivetrain for an “EV-like” experience and a small gas engine that serves as a generator to charge the battery when it gets low.
The new Santa Fe EREV will be built at Hyundai’s manufacturing plant in Alabama and sold in the US.
Hyundai plans to launch its first EREV in 2027 (Source: Hyundai)
New batteries, software, and other advanced tech
It will be powered by Hyundai’s new in-house battery cells, which the company said deliver more than double the output of its previous high-nickel cells. They also cut charging time by 40%.
The new high-performance cells will debut in the EREV in the first half of 2027. Hyundai said new EVs will launch next year with mid-nickel NCM cells that slash battery costs by about 30%.
Hyundai plans to launch 10 new hybrid vehicles in North America by 2030, starting with the
Genesis GV80 Hybrid
, set to launch in September.
Hyundai new vehicle roadmap (Source: Hyundai)
In Europe, Hyundai will cover 85% of the market with a fully electrified lineup, including five new SUVs and light commercial vehicles. By 2030, Hyundai aims to sell 420,000 EVs in Europe, up from 116,000 last year.
Hyundai’s first compact EV from its IONIQ series, the IONIQ 3,
went on sale
this month. The electric hatch offers 309 miles (497 km) of range and is Hyundai’s first vehicle in Europe equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment platform.
Korea will serve as “the cradle of Hyundai Motor’s global growth” with new manufacturing innovations.
Genesis GV90 debut (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek)
The flagship Genesis GV90, which Hyundai revealed in San Francisco last week (
see our photos from the event
), will go into production at Hyundai’s new Ulsan EV plant.
As a software-defined factory (SSF), Hyundai’s Ulsan EV plant uses 108 advanced manufacturing methods, including AI quality control and inspection.
In China, Hyundai will lean on local partnerships as part of its comeback plans. Starting with the IONIQ V, the company will introduce new vehicles, including another EV and an EREV in 2027. By 2030, Hyundai plans to sell over 500,000 vehicles in China.
Chang Hwan Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of Electrification Energy Solutions Tech Unit at Hyundai Motor Group (Source: Hyundai)
Genesis expands into new luxury segments
Genesis, on the other hand, has “grown faster than any luxury marque in history” over the past decade, Muñoz said.
Over the next decade, Genesis plans to establish itself as a true global luxury powerhouse. The GV90 and new hybrid options will enable it to tap into some of the hottest segments in the luxury space.
The flagship GV90 embodies everything Genesis has to offer in terms of luxury and technology, which will eventually trickle down into other vehicles and segments.
Q&A at Hyundai’s 2026 CEO Investor Day (Source: Hyundai)
To support the aggressive product blitz, Hyundai will expand global production capacity to 1.27 million units by 2030.
This includes 500,000 units in North America, 320,000 units in India, 200,000 units in Korea, and 250,000 units for CKD production.

title: How Tesla's solar business works in 2026 after killing Solar Roof
content:
Tesla Solar Roof
tesla solar
powerwall
Fred Lambert
| Aug 26 2026 - 7:55 am PT
Tesla’s residential solar business has been shrinking for most of a decade, ever since the company absorbed SolarCity in 2016. Now, with electricity rates climbing across the US, Tesla is trying to revive it around a new in-house solar panel and Powerwall 3 — while quietly retiring the product it was once best known for.
Earlier this month, Tesla
discontinued its Solar Roof
, the glass solar tile it launched in 2016. It was always a tiny piece of the business, and its end says more about where Tesla solar is going than where it’s been.
When Tesla bought SolarCity for roughly $2.6 billion in 2016, it inherited the largest residential solar installer in the country. It didn’t stay that way.
Tesla’s quarterly solar deployments have fallen for years, and the company eventually scaled back how much it discloses about the segment. Its overall energy business is booming, Tesla reported $12.8 billion in energy revenue in 2025, up 27% year over year, but that growth is almost entirely driven by battery storage like Megapack and Powerwall, not rooftop solar.
Solar Roof was the clearest example of the struggle. Despite years of promotion, Tesla had installed only about 3,000 of the tile roofs in the US by the end of 2022, accounting for roughly 0.17% of residential solar installations that year. It was expensive, slow to install, and never scaled. A surface view of Tesla’s energy business might lead you to think that killing solar roof amid a scale-down of its solar business means Tesla is walking away from solar, but that’s not the case.
What Tesla sells now
The centerpiece is a new panel. In
January 2026, Tesla launched a US-made 420-watt solar panel
assembled at its Gigafactory in Buffalo, New York — the same plant that used to build Solar Roof tiles. Tesla says it’s the first solar panel the company has fully designed and manufactured itself, with an all-black look, integrated mounting, and better performance in shade.
The panel is designed to pair with Powerwall 3, which combines the home battery and solar inverter in one unit. On Tesla’s design tool, the default configuration is now solar panels bundled with a Powerwall 3, and the whole experience is built around storing energy for outages and rising time-of-use rates.
Solar-only is still an option, Tesla’s configurator lets you drop the battery, but Powerwall is pre-selected, and much of the current pitch is about backup power and energy independence rather than solar alone.
Tesla’s online design tool now leads with a Solar Panels + Powerwall 3 bundle. (Source: Tesla)
Who actually installs it
This is where Tesla solar has changed the most, and where it gets confusing for buyers.
Tesla is stepping back from doing its own installations. In
September 2024, the company began recruiting third-party “Certified Installers”
as it wound down its in-house solar crews. Tesla’s own support pages now describe a hybrid model: “Tesla works with trained Certified Installers to install our home energy and charging products in areas where Tesla does not directly install.”
That network has grown quickly. Tesla counted about 2,000 certified installers across 14 countries in late 2024. Today, its partner page lists more than 7,000 installers in 35-plus countries and over 1 million installations. These companies buy Tesla hardware, quote and install it, and handle service, all running on Tesla’s “Tesla One” software platform.
So there are effectively two ways to get Tesla solar. In Tesla’s own “direct service territories,” Tesla sells and installs the system with its own crews. The scale of that operation is unclear. Everywhere else, you buy Tesla equipment, but a certified installer designs, prices, installs, and services it.
Where it’s available — and why that’s hard to answer
Tesla no longer publishes a list of states where it installs directly. The company doesn’t tell you which model applies to you until you enter your address in its online design tool.
The sales side is effectively national. Tesla’s configurator generates instant quotes and takes a $100 refundable deposit to start an order in states across the country, with a base cash price around $2.30 per watt before installation and incentives. Financing is standardized too: solar loans around 7.24%, Powerwall loans around 6.99%, and leases around 8.5%.
Tesla’s configurator returns an instant quote with cash, lease, and financing options and pushes the lease as the “lowest monthly price.” (Source: Tesla)
The install and financing side is where geography matters. Tesla’s lease, a 25-year solar lease (12 years for Powerwall-only) with a buyout option after five years and a 3% annual price escalator, is offered only in Tesla’s direct service territories, according to the company’s support pages. Within a given state, availability of leases and utility incentives can also vary by utility, which is part of why Tesla keeps the map vague and steers everyone to the address-based tool.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla solar in 2026 is a different business than the one it was five years ago. Tesla has essentially decided it wants to be a solar manufacturer and technology provider, panels from Buffalo, Powerwall as the hub, software to run the network, rather than the national installer it inherited from SolarCity.
Installation is a low-margin, labor-heavy, local business, and Tesla was never good at scaling it profitably. Handing it to 7,000-plus certified installers lets Tesla sell hardware and keep its energy software inside the home without owning the trucks and crews. Ending Solar Roof, a product that never cracked a fraction of a percent of the market, fits the same logic.
The trade-off lands on buyers. The experience you get now depends heavily on whether you’re in a Tesla direct market or handed to a third party, and Tesla makes it deliberately hard to know which one you’re in until you’re deep in the quote flow.
One thing is clear: it looks like Tesla still wants to be part of the solar business in the US.
Rising electricity rates are the best argument for going solar right now, but the price and experience you get depends a lot on who installs your system. Since Tesla now routes most of its installations through third-party partners, it’s worth shopping around.

title: Tesla denies rumors it's abandoning 'Full Self-Driving' push in China
content:
autonomous driving
Fred Lambert
| Aug 26 2026 - 6:46 am PT
Tesla is denying rumors that it has pulled its “Full Self-Driving” team out of China, saying its Shanghai data center is “operating normally” and that it has even reported the claims to police.
The denial comes as China remains conspicuously absent from Tesla’s own list of markets where customers can subscribe to FSD because of the regulatory limbo the driver assist system faces.
What the rumors claimed
Rumors circulated on Chinese social media on Tuesday claiming that Tesla’s Shanghai data center — set up specifically to prepare the ground for a “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” launch in China — had been vacated, its liaison teams withdrawn, and related positions eliminated.
The speculation fed a broader narrative that Tesla is quietly retreating from its long-delayed effort to bring FSD to the world’s largest EV market.
Tesla China pushed back hard. Responding to Chinese outlets Tencent Tech and National Business Daily on Wednesday, the company said the Shanghai data center “is operating normally,” that recruitment for driver-assistance roles is actually accelerating, and that the work is “progressing steadily,” according to
CnEVPost
Tesla also said it reported the rumors to police — an aggressive move that signals how sensitive the automaker is about any suggestion that its China FSD effort has stalled.
The problem is the market list
China does not appear on Tesla’s updated list of 12 markets where FSD (Supervised) subscriptions are offered — a list that includes the US, Canada, Australia, South Korea, and several European countries. Yet Tesla’s US website still lists China among markets where FSD Supervised is “available for use.”
That contradiction has been the through-line of Tesla’s China autonomy story all year. Tesla announced FSD availability in China back in May 2026, then renamed the software “Tesla Assisted Driving” on its Chinese site. But it has never published subscription pricing or a broad rollout timeline for Chinese customers.
We reported in February that
Tesla secured AI training capability inside China
, a genuine and necessary step given Beijing’s rules on keeping data local. And we covered in January how
Chinese regulators shut down Elon Musk’s claim that FSD would be approved “next month”
. The pattern of announced progress meeting regulatory reality has been consistent.
Local rivals aren’t waiting
While Tesla manages rumors, Chinese automakers are shipping. Domestic players including Xiaomi and Huawei have been rapidly expanding urban driver-assistance features that operate on city streets across China — the exact capability Tesla is still trying to get cleared.
Xpeng is preparing to launch an upgraded version of its own level 2 driver-assist system, which is already competitive with Tesla’s nerfed version of FSD in China.
That competitive gap is what makes the rumors sticky. Tesla’s China business is under pressure from a wave of cheaper, feature-rich local EVs, and its assisted-driving software was supposed to be a differentiator. Every month without a clear FSD rollout is a month rivals use to entrench.
Electrek’s Take
There’s no solid evidence Tesla shut down its Shanghai data center, and reporting rumors to police is a standard corporate move in China, where authorities take a hard line on market-moving misinformation. Something that would put Tesla’s own CEO in trouble if it were the other way around.
But the denial doesn’t answer the question that actually matters: when will Chinese owners be able to use the full FSD product? Tesla saying recruitment is “accelerating” and work is “progressing steadily” is the same forward-looking language we’ve heard for over a year, and China is still missing from the subscription market list while sitting awkwardly on the US site as “available.”
The most likely reading is that Tesla is stuck in the same regulatory limbo it’s been in since January — data localization solved, but a wide urban FSD release still gated by Beijing’s approval process. Denying a pullout is easy.

title: New electric Flyer promises 15 minute service from Chicago to O'Hare
content:
Electric train
Jo Borrás
| Aug 26 2026 - 4:46 am PT
A group of Chicago business leaders have announced plan to launch what they’re calling, “the first airport express train in the US.” The O’Hare Flyer is a fully electric train that will offer non-stop rides between downtown Chicago and America’s busiest airfield.
The planned
fully electric train
route has been pieced together, Ticket to Ride-style, using freight rail right-of-way currently owned by three Class I railroads: CSX,
Canadian National (CN)
, and Union Pacific (UP). The O’Hare Flyer group has signed a Letter of Intent (LOI) with
and says it’s moving forward with the other carriers as well.
“By combining three existing but underused freight rights-of-way into a dedicated express rail service, we will create the best airport transportation experience in America – and one of the best in the world,” remarked O’Hare Flyer Founder and Chief Engineering Officer, Mark Walbrun. “This is an important first for Chicago and for the country. O’Hare Flyer will build on Chicago’s heritage as America’s rail capital and center of innovation.”
The proposed train would carry passengers from
‘s West Loop to O’Hare’s Terminal 2, which serves Air Canada, JetBlue, United Express, and select United Airlines flights. Alaska Airlines and select Delta flights also operate from the terminal.
Easier, faster
O’Hare Flyer passenger places her luggage.
Chicago Tribune
editorial published along with the announcement projects a $25-35 cost (per passenger) to ride the proposed express train –
which we can’t help but compare to the slower existing CTA Blue Line route from Terminal 1 that costs $2.50 and makes stops throughout the NW suburbs
– and claims trains will leave O’Hare every 15 minutes, on the quarter hour.
It’s important to note, also, that the O’Hare Flyer is a private, commercial endeavor, and the group behind it says they’re not currently seeking government subsidies or funding that could otherwise go to regional transit agencies such as Chicago’s existing CTA or Metra rail services. And, in addition to bringing their own money to the table, the group is also planning to bring union jobs to the area.
“O’Hare Flyer will be a job creation engine and an investment in working families and communities across Greater Chicago,” says Mike Macellaio, President of the Chicago and Cook County Building and Construction Trades Council. “Our MOU is an important first step toward a Project Labor Agreement that will help ensure this landmark project is built by Greater Chicago’s highly skilled unionized construction workforce while expanding opportunities for local workers and delivering lasting economic benefits throughout the region.”
The O’Hare Flyer team plans to have the first trains in operation around 2030, and is currently meeting with public officials, business, finance, government, and community groups to promote the project.

title: Japan’s Tokuyama opens polysilicon factory in Vietnam - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The facility, located in Ho Chi Minh City, will manufacture and distribute polysilicon for semiconductors.
Patrick Jowett
26 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Manufacturing
polysilicon
Japanese chemical producer Tokuyama has inaugurated a polysilicon factory in Vietnam.
Plans for the factory were first announced
. Located within the Phu My 3 Special Industrial Park in Ho Chi Minh City, the facility will manufacture and distribute polysilicon for semiconductors.
“With the semiconductor market expected to expand further, we aim to ensure a stable supply of silicon wafer raw materials used in advanced semiconductors and strengthen the supply chain, and [the facility] will be an important overseas base responsible for the crushing and cleaning of polycrystalline silicon,” a statement on the company’s website explains.
The company adds that the facility will proceed with trial operators and quality checks with safety as its top priority. Total capital invested into the project reached VND 580 billion ($22.2 million).
Tokuyama says the factory is Vietnam’s first in the manufacture and distributor of polycrystalline silicon for semiconductors. While the company has not disclosed the capacity of the facility, local press has reported it will have an annual production capacity of 4,995 MT of polysilicon.
Last year, Tokuyama began building a 10,000 MT
polysilicon factory in Malaysia
in partnership with South Korea-based polysilicon producer OCI.
OCIM Sdn Bhd, the Malaysian unit of OCI, is currently operating a
35,000 MT polysilicon factory
in the Samalaju Industrial Park in Sarawak, Malaysia, which it bought from Tokuyama in 2016.

title: Spain to require data centers to source 80% of electricity from renewables - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Spain has proposed new rules requiring data centers to source at least 80% of their electricity from additional renewable generation, with hourly matching of consumption and supply. The framework would apply to facilities of at least 1 MW and introduce grid access, water efficiency and EU data sovereignty requirements.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
26 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
On August 25, Spain’s Council of Ministers approved the urgent administrative processing of a draft royal decree that would establish a new regulatory framework for data center development, linking expansion to energy sustainability, water efficiency, resilience and digital sovereignty requirements.
Under the proposed rules, data centers would have to be operated by entities established in the European Union. Operators would be required to keep infrastructure-related operational data within EU territory and take measures to prevent access by authorities in third countries where such access is not authorized under EU law.
Data centers above specified thresholds would have to submit declarations confirming compliance with the requirements. Facilities hosting public administration or national security data would also have to formally guarantee that the data remains within the European Union.
The Spanish government said more than 12 GW of grid access and connection rights have been granted to data centers since 2021.
Renewable electricity
The draft decree would require data centers to certify that at least 80% of their electricity consumption comes from renewable sources. The requirement would remain in place until renewables account for more than 90% of Spain’s electricity mix, after which the threshold could be revised.
The renewable electricity would also have to meet an additionality requirement. Contracting existing renewable generation would not be sufficient. Each new megawatt of electricity demand associated with a data center would have to be matched by 1 MW of new renewable generation capacity commissioned no more than 18 months before the data center begins operating.
The additional capacity could come from on-site generation or long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs).
Hourly matching
The proposal would also introduce hourly matching requirements for renewable electricity consumption. During each hour of operation, renewable generation produced in the same hour would have to cover at least 80% of a data center’s electricity consumption.
The requirement goes beyond systems based on guarantees of origin or annual electricity matching, as operators would have to account for the hourly profiles of both data center demand and contracted renewable generation.
The requirement could encourage the deployment of energy storage to shift renewable generation between periods, although the draft does not explicitly require battery storage.
Grid access requirements
Data center projects seeking grid access would have to demonstrate compliance with the new requirements to obtain access and connection rights. Failure to comply could result in progressively higher charges and tariffs and, ultimately, the loss of grid access rights.
The mechanism is designed to allocate to developers part of the system costs associated with failure to meet the additionality and hourly matching requirements.
Data centers already in the permitting process would have six months to comply with the new requirements. Projects awaiting a grid access tender would have three months.
Developers could alternatively relinquish their grid access and connection rights without losing the associated financial guarantees.
1 MW threshold and water efficiency
The draft decree would apply the specific requirements to data centers with electrical capacity of at least 1 MW, reflecting their potential impact on local areas, water resources and the electricity system.
Data centers would also have to meet the highest energy and water efficiency standards under the European Union’s forthcoming labeling system for such facilities. Once the European framework takes effect, data centers covered by the royal decree would be required to achieve a Category A rating for both energy and water efficiency.

title: AI optimizer to trade Baltic hybrid solar-storage assets - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Finnish battery optimizer Capalo AI has partnered with Danish developer European Energy to provide trading and market-access services for two hybrid solar-plus-storage projects in Lithuania and Latvia.
Brian Publicover
26 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Capalo AI, a Finnish company that optimizes battery energy storage systems across European electricity markets, has agreed to provide route-to-market and trading services for two hybrid solar-plus-storage projects owned by Danish developer European Energy in the Baltic region.
The first asset is the Anykščiai hybrid project in Lithuania, comprising a 78.5 MW solar park co-located with a battery connected in June 2026 at 25 MW/65 MWh. European Energy had
previously announced financing for a 50 MW battery
at the same site, but it is unclear from public disclosures whether the 25 MW/65 MWh system represents the final project configuration, a phased deployment, or a change from earlier financing plans. Capalo AI’s release describes commissioning and market prequalification for the asset as finalized in August 2026.
The second asset is the Saldus Hybrid Park in Latvia, where Capalo AI and European Energy describe the battery component as 46 MW/105 MWh. The project remains under construction.
European Energy’s own prior announcements have described the battery differently: an October 2025 announcement of European Energy’s sale of a 50% stake in the project to Danish pension fund Sampension cited a 46 MW rating, while a November 2025 financing announcement cited 92 MWh. It is not clear from public disclosures whether these figures describe the same final configuration as the newly announced 105 MWh.
Capalo AI said it will provide day-ahead, intraday and balancing-market trading, along with coordinated dispatch of the solar and battery components as a single flexible unit. The company also said it will provide balance responsible party (BRP) services for the Baltic assets. In Poland, by contrast, Capalo AI holds its own
electricity-trading license
but a third party, AARX Energy, serves as BRP, indicating the role can vary by market.
Capalo AI manages 1.6 GW of batteries and 460 MWp of solar under its
Zeus VPP platform
, with 600 MW and 300 MWp of that already live under trading and optimization. The company, founded in 2022, now operates in six European markets and plans to expand into five more this year. It also raised €11 million ($12.8 million) in a Series A round led by Heartcore Capital earlier this year.
Henri Taskinen, Capalo AI’s CEO, noted that European Energy has a large renewable-energy development portfolio. He said that Capalo AI expects the Anykščiai and Saldus assets to participate in Baltic balancing and wholesale power markets through its optimization platform.
European Energy Deputy CEO Jens-Peter Zink said battery storage and the hybridization of energy parks is becoming an increasingly important part of the company’s portfolio, and added that the Baltic countries are a particularly interesting market.
European Energy, headquartered in Copenhagen, reported €766 million in revenue and €170 million in EBITDA for 2025, with 662 MW of renewable capacity grid-connected during the year and a battery-storage development pipeline that grew from 2.4 GW to 7.4 GW over the same period.
The Baltic states have moved toward common regional balancing arrangements since synchronizing with Continental Europe, with Lithuania becoming one of the region’s most active battery storage markets. The country’s government has approved support for up to approximately
1.7 GW/4 GWh of new storage capacity

Southampton FC fans can access discounted rooftop solar panels through leasing company Utilita Home, with potential annual energy savings and a chance to win match tickets and a signed shirt.

Southampton FC has teamed up with Utilita to offer fans a buy one, get one free solar promotion.
Southampton FC fans who spy an opportunity to improve their household energy efficiency are being offered a buy one, get one free discount on solar panels via UK solar leasing company Utilita Home.
New customers looking to score discounted rooftop solar panels are invited to apply for a free online quote from Utilita Home using promotional offer code. To qualify for the promotion, entrants must be new domestic solar customers aged 18, and must complete and submit a desktop survey. Eligibility for promotion is subject to terms and conditions.
Southampton FC is not the only English club with ties to the solar industry. Premier League runners-up Manchester City signed a multi-year global partnership with JinkSolar in June 2024.

title: Ecoprogetti upgrades PV module line in South Africa - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The solar equipment manufacturer completed a project rescue on a PV module line in South Africa that previously faced integration challenges. The newly-operational 200 MW line produces modules primarily for the local market.
Patrick Jowett
26 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Highlights
Manufacturing
South Africa
Italian PV equipment manufacturer Ecoprogetti has upgraded an existing PV module manufacturing line in South Africa.
The company explained its upgrade follows an initial installation carried out by a different supplier which had left the production line with integration challenges and unable to reach expected output levels.
A spokesperson for Ecoprogetti told
pv magazine
the upgraded manufacturing facility has an increased nominal annual production capacity reaching approximately 200 MW.
“The line is designed to manufacture different module formats depending on the intended application,” the spokesperson said. “This includes high-power PV modules of up to 650 W, mainly for larger-scale installations and solar parks, as well as modules of around 500 W for off-grid and stand-alone applications.”
Ecoprogetti says it delivered the upgrade through key phases including a detailed technical assessment and identification of critical issues.
It supplied advanced testing equipment, including the latest-generation Ecosun Nova solar simulator and Ecolab EL electroluminescence testers for in-line module testing and quality control, as well as an automatic interconnection machine, Ecobussing, for automatic cell interconnection soldering. The company then offered IEC certification support and on-site services during installation and restart phases.
The production line is now fully installed and operational. Ecoprogetti’s spokesperson also told
pv magazine
production is primarily intended for the South African local market, with target applications including solar parks, agriculture, rural electrification and off-grid installations.
“In particular, the smaller modules are suitable for stand-alone systems serving local homes and agricultural applications, including solar-powered water pumping,” the spokesperson added. “The facility is therefore positioned to support both larger solar projects and decentralized energy solutions for local communities and the agricultural sector.”
Ecoprogetti CEO Laura Sartore commented that a project rescue is not simply about fixing a problem but stepping into a critical situation, restoring control and performance, and delivering tangible value back to the client and investors.
“What truly matters is ensuring continuous output of high-quality PV modules, and this is what we consistently guarantee as a turnkey line provider and PV process expert,” Sartore said.
Ecoprogetti added that Africa represents a key strategic market. The company has also been expanding in the Middle East, most recently with
Iraq’s first solar module production line
and previously with
production lines in Oman

title: Endesa tests voltage control system to integrate more low-voltage self-consumption - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Endesa’s distribution unit, e-distribución, is testing a voltage control system on low-voltage grids in Aragon and the Balearic Islands. The technology is designed to manage voltage fluctuations and increase grid capacity for self-consumption, renewables and EV charging.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
26 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Endesa is testing a new solution to improve low-voltage grid stability as self-consumption deployment increases in Spain.
The growing adoption of self-consumption and distributed generation is changing power flows in low-voltage grids in Spain, increasing the need to monitor and manage electrical parameters in real time. E-distribución, the distribution arm of Spanish utility
, is testing the LV Line Manager, a system designed to control voltage levels and facilitate the connection of new energy resources while maintaining supply quality.
The device provides real-time monitoring and management of voltage on low-voltage networks. Its deployment comes as electricity generation increasingly shifts from centralized power plants toward distributed generation closer to points of consumption.
E-distribución’s network currently serves more than 438,500 connected self-consumption installations, including around 45,000 collective systems. The resulting bidirectional electricity flows pose new technical challenges for distribution networks.
The pilot will be deployed on networks in Aragon and the Balearic Islands to assess the LV Line Manager’s performance under conditions associated with distributed generation and fluctuating demand.
One challenge is overvoltage during periods of high photovoltaic generation, particularly around midday. Demand peaks, meanwhile, can cause voltage drops. Networks can also experience voltage imbalances due to the uneven distribution of users and differences in their consumption and generation profiles.
The system continuously monitors electrical parameters, including voltage and current, and can automatically intervene to correct imbalances and maintain grid conditions within operating limits.
It is also designed to facilitate the connection of additional low-voltage resources, including renewable energy systems and electric vehicle charging infrastructure.
E-distribución said the technology could increase the capacity of existing networks to accommodate additional distributed energy resources while reducing voltage quality issues.
Real-time voltage management could allow distribution operators to make greater use of existing infrastructure and increase grid flexibility in response to fluctuations in generation and demand.
The LV Line Manager was developed as part of an
Enel Group
innovation project involving different grid environments in Italy and Spain. Enel selected the technology through its Open Innovability platform after evaluating market-ready solutions for testing under real-world grid conditions.

title: Hinen launches 13.68 kWh residential energy storage system - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Hinen’s A15 residential energy storage system combines 3.6 kW to 15 kW hybrid inverters with 14.4 kWh LFP battery modules, each offering 13.68 kWh of usable capacity. Up to six batteries can be connected in parallel for 86.4 kWh nominal and 82.08 kWh usable capacity, with more than 8,000 cycles, IP65 protection and a 12-year warranty.
Tristan Rayner
26 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
A Hinen A15 installation shown on YouTube
China-based inverter and energy storage system provider
has launched its A15 residential energy storage system in the United Kingdom. The system combines hybrid inverters with modular, high-voltage lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries.
The A15 pairs Hinen’s A-series hybrid inverters with its B15 high-voltage battery module. Each B15 module has a nominal capacity of 14.4 kWh and an initial usable capacity of 13.68 kWh. Up to six battery modules can be connected in parallel, providing up to 86.4 kWh of nominal capacity and 82.08 kWh of usable capacity.
Each B15 battery weighs 117 kg and is equipped with handles. The system is compatible with Hinen’s single-phase and three-phase A-series hybrid inverters. Single-phase models are available with power ratings ranging from 3.6 kW to 15 kW.
The 3.6 kW inverter option falls within the scope of the United Kingdom’s G98 connection process, under which qualifying systems can generally be installed before the distribution network operator (DNO) is notified. Higher-power systems may require a different grid-connection process, depending on the installation and DNO requirements.
The A15 has a depth of 180 mm and can be installed in garages, utility rooms and other areas where space is limited. It supports wall- and floor-mounted installation, with adjustable feet available for floor mounting.
Hinen said the battery is rated for more than 8,000 cycles and comes with a 12-year warranty. The company said the system does not require an external battery management system (BMS), reducing the amount of wiring required during installation.
The battery incorporates a heating system designed to enable operation at temperatures as low as -20 C. The system has an IP65 enclosure and what Hinen describes as a five-layer protection system.
According to Hinen, the A15 also includes a built-in circuit breaker, automatic fault isolation designed to allow continued operation if an individual battery module fails, and an internal aerosol fire-suppression system.
Users can monitor real-time energy consumption through the Hinen app, which also supports over-the-air (OTA) firmware updates. The system can be used for applications including solar self-consumption and supplying loads such as electric vehicle chargers and heat pumps.
“The UK is an important market for Hinen. The A15 launch marks more than a new product – it strengthens our commitment to local partnerships and the support network needed to help installers and homeowners adopt energy storage with confidence,” said Dustin Wang, country general manager at Hinen UK.
Hinen unveiled the A15 during an online event aimed at installers. Participants included the company’s technical team, UK distributors and installers, industry representatives and homeowners. The event featured installation and commissioning demonstrations, information on Hinen’s experience in the Australian market, and introductory pricing for installers.

title: Indonesia aims for 100 GW solar target by 2029 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has said the government is serious about realizing its 100 GW solar program, with construction targeted within three years.
Patrick Jowett
26 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Highlights
Indonesia
President Subianto launching the program
The Indonesian government has officially launched its
100 GW solar power plant program
Speaking during a groundbreaking ceremony, President Prabowo Subianto said the government is serious about realizing the program and is aiming to develop 100 GW within three years.
According to a statement published by the government, the program will be carried out in phases with the initial phase targeting 17 GW of new capacity.
Under this first phase, 14 solar plants with a combined capacity of 5.2 GW are already in various stages of development. Reports from Reuters add that two of these plants are already in operation, with six in the construction phase and another six to be offered to investors.
Indonesia’s flagship solar program will target the deployment of ground-mounted, rooftop and floating solar power plants, as well as decentralized, smaller-scale solar systems, in order to replace diesel generation, electrify rural areas and villages and strengthen the country’s energy security and independence.
The program will also deploy battery energy storage systems (BESS) in efforts to support a more reliable power system. The official launch of the program coincided with the start of construction of a 305 MW solar project alongside a 1 GWh BESS in the port town of Gilimanuk, west Bali. The project belongs to Indonesia’s power utility PLN.
The 100 GW target surpasses Indonesia’s current electricity generation capacity, which stands at around 88 GW. According to the country’s Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources, Bahlil Lahadalia, it will require approximately $73 billion in investment and has the potential to create over 5.5 million jobs.
In a statement sent to
pv magazine
, Indonesian think tank Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR) said that achieving the 100 GW target in less than four years is highly ambitious and will require innovative approaches to implementation.
“For the program to succeed, Indonesia needs a strong and consistent national implementation architecture backed by regulatory certainty,” IESR said. “The government must immediately establish clear program leadership with the authority to coordinate across ministries, PLN, local governments, industry, financial institutions, and businesses.”
IESR’s Chief Executive Officer, Fabby Tumiwa, added that success of the program should not be measured by how many projects break ground, but by how many gigawatts of solar can be built, connected to the grid, and reliably generate electricity before 2029.
“The biggest challenge now is to translate the President’s political commitment into an implementation engine capable of delivering tens of gigawatts of solar PV every year,” Tumiwa added.
IESR is recommending six priority measures to ensure the program achieves its 100 GW target, beginning with immediately finalzing a presidential regulation as the legal framework for the program, and aligning the country’s national energy general plan and PLN’s electricity supply business plan to accommodate the additional capacity.
It also recommends developing a clear annual project pipeline through 2029, accelerating procurement through competitive, transparent, and bankable tenders, ensuring power system readiness, developing a national supply chain and adopting a multi-track implementation so the program is not solely dependent on PLN projects.
Earlier this year, IESR released a report exploring how Indonesia can
mobilize its 100 GW solar target
as it warned against trying to adopt a one-size-fits all approach to electrifying the 80,000 villages targeted by the program.
